analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.25 over three years and expands the earned income tax credit, with new exemptions for small businesses and tipped workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced June 14, 1989 with 51 cosponsors, it was referred to two committees and then a subcommittee, and it died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps from $3.35 to $4.25 an hour by 1992 and made the earned income tax credit — a tax credit for low-income working families — larger and available to more children, with annual inflation adjustments. To offset the cost to employers, it also would have exempted businesses with under $500,000 in annual sales from minimum wage and overtime rules, let employers count tips toward half the minimum wage instead of 40 percent, and allowed a lower starting wage for new hires. It applied minimum wage protections to House of Representatives employees for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers at covered businesses would get step increases to $4.25 an hour by 1992, and working parents with children would get a larger earned income tax credit, including extra amounts per school-age and preschool child. Workers at businesses newly exempted would not benefit, and tipped workers would gain less.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.65 in 1990, $3.95 in 1991, and $4.25 in 1992 and after [S2] [S3].

Expands the earned income tax credit: the credit rate rises from 14 to 15 percent on up to $7,000 of earnings, with an added 5 percent per school-age child and 10 percent per preschool child (up to four children), and the amounts are indexed to inflation starting in 1992 [S2] [S3].
Repeals a provision of the Family Support Act of 1988 that counted the earned income credit against welfare benefits, so families would keep the full credit [S2] [S3].
Extends Fair Labor Standards Act minimum wage and overtime protections to House of Representatives employees and Architect of the Capitol employees [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers would bear higher wage bills, likely passed to consumers through prices. Workers at businesses falling under the new $500,000 exemption would lose minimum wage and overtime coverage, and tipped workers would have a weaker wage floor because employers could count more of their tips toward the minimum.
analysis.who_pays_short: Covered employers, small-business employees, tipped workers

drawbacks.text: Raising the tip credit from 40 to 50 percent lets employers count more of a tipped worker's tips toward the minimum wage, weakening the effective wage floor for restaurant and hotel workers [S2].
Exempting enterprises with annual sales under $500,000 (up from $362,500) would remove minimum wage and overtime protections from workers at newly exempt businesses [S2] [S3].
A new-hire provision lets employers pay new employees $3.35 an hour — later 80 percent of the minimum — for up to 120 days, creating a legal subminimum for beginners [S2] [S3].

Employers could skip overtime pay for up to 10 hours a week if the employee is in remedial basic-skills education, and the bill narrows the dependent care credit for families with children under 15 unless they give up the larger earned income credit [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — a higher minimum wage and a bigger earned income tax credit — would meaningfully help low-wage workers and working families. But the bill pays for the wage increase partly by shrinking protections: tipped workers and employees at small exempt businesses would end up with weaker floors than current law, and new hires could legally be paid less. It reads as a Republican compromise alternative to the Democrats' minimum wage bill, trading a smaller or slower raise for business exemptions.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: after introduction it was sent to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor Committees, then in July 1989 to the Labor Standards subcommittee, and it never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Goodling (R-PA) introduced the bill on June 14, 1989, joined by 51 Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The same day it was referred to the House Ways and Means and Education and Labor Committees [S5].

On July 12, 1989 it was referred to the Education and Labor Committee's Subcommittee on Labor Standards, and no further action was recorded before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the higher wage floor and lost the proposed small-business and tip-credit exemptions were better off with the bill dead. Low-wage workers got nothing from this bill, though a separate minimum wage increase to $4.25 by 1991, without the small-business exemption or the larger tip credit, became law later in 1989.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the bill's terms

for.name: Rep. William Goodling (R-PA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Living Wage Act, pairing a minimum wage increase and earned income tax credit expansion with small-business exemptions

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski, D-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 14, 1989 and took no recorded action on the bill

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee / Subcommittee on Labor Standards
against.role: Committee and subcommittee of referral (chair: Rep. Augustus Hawkins, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Labor Standards subcommittee on July 12, 1989; no markup or floor action followed

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Advanced its own minimum wage bill instead of this Republican alternative; this bill never reached the floor

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 51 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-run committees that controlled the bill's path took no action; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Small businesses under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: The bill raises the small-business exemption threshold from $362,500 to $500,000, removing minimum wage and overtime coverage from their employees. That is a direct cost to the workers those businesses employ.

industries.industry: Restaurants and other employers of tipped workers
industries.note: Raising the tip credit from 40 to 50 percent lets these employers count more of workers' tips toward the minimum wage, lowering their cash wage obligations. Tipped workers bear the difference.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers generally (retail, services, small manufacturing)
industries.note: They face step increases in the minimum wage to $4.25 by 1992, but the bill offsets this with a 120-day subminimum for new hires and an overtime exemption of up to 10 hours a week for employees in remedial education.
